the incidence of contrast induced nephropathy (25% increase in creatinine) was 2.9%, and the incidence of chronic renal disease or dialysis was zero.

none of the 198 acute stroke patients developed chronic kidney failure, and only 5 of 175 patients (2.9% of the entire group, and 2% of those with no known renal impairment) developed contrast-induced nephropathies after undergoing CTA/CT perfusion studies for evaluation of their acute stroke.

1) none of the 198 acute stroke patients developed chronic kidney failure or required dialysis; 2) 2.9% developed CIN; and 3) 2% of patients developed CIN when scanned before baseline creatinine levels were available.

the development of a new generation of contrast agents for medical imaging, with the aim to reduce the risk of renal damage.
the study of the safety of the contrast medium used during CT angiography and CT perfusion in patients with acute stroke.
the study of the safety of the use of iodine contrast media for CT scanning in the acute stroke patient population, specifically in those with no baseline renal function data available.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CTA/CTp imaging is safe in acute ischemic stroke patients with normal renal function.
CT angiography is not associated with a significant increase in the incidence of acute renal failure in patients with acute stroke.
the incidence of renal sequel is relatively low in patients undergoing emergent CTA/CT perfusion imaging for acute stroke.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the incidence of renal sequel after emergent CT perfusion and CT angiography in the acute stroke setting was relatively low, and the results support that these studies should not be delayed in patients with no history of kidney disease or renal impairment.
the incidence of CIN is relatively low in the acute stroke patient undergoing emergent CTA/CTA.
the use of CTP and CTA in the acute stroke setting does not appear to be associated with a high rate of renal dysfunction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in the acute stroke setting, the incidence of CIN in the setting of emergent contrast CT scanning is low, even when baseline creatinine levels are unknown.
the incidence of contrast-related renal impairment is relatively low in patients who undergo CTA and CTP for the evaluation of acute stroke.

the incidence of renal sequel in acute stroke patients who undergo emergent CTA/CTp is low, and that prompt scanning of acute stroke patients, if indicated, can be performed without delay in patients with no known history of renal disease.
